# Digestion and absorption

> *A sachet of glucose and salt can rehydrate a child with severe diarrhoea, because one transporter
> in the gut wall keeps working while the gut pours out fluid. The nutrients in a meal enter the body
> by crossing that same wall, most of them only after digestion has broken them into pieces small
> enough to cross.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Trace a meal through the gut and its four accessory organs, naming where starch, protein and fat are
  digested and by which enzymes.
- Explain how motility moves food along, how the gut hormones time each stage of digestion, and why
  pancreatic bicarbonate is needed.
- Distinguish lactase deficiency, lactose intolerance and milk allergy.
- Explain how glucose is absorbed alongside sodium, and why oral rehydration salts need both.
- Describe how bile, micelles and chylomicrons carry fat into the lymph, and explain why damage to the
  terminal ileum can cause both fat malabsorption and vitamin B12 deficiency.
- Explain how a food's form, cooking and meal order change the speed of digestion, and recognise
  food–drug interactions to refer to a pharmacist.
:::

## Digestion and absorption at a glance {#sec-overview}

The gut is one continuous tube from mouth to anus, so whatever is inside it is still, in a sense,
outside the body. Food enters the body only when its nutrients cross the gut wall, and the digestive
system therefore has two jobs:

Digestion
: Breaking food into pieces small enough to absorb.

Absorption
: Moving those pieces across the gut wall into the blood or lymph.

The tube runs from the mouth through the oesophagus, stomach and small intestine to the large
intestine. Four **accessory organs** pour their juices into it along the way: the salivary glands, the
liver, the gallbladder and the pancreas. Most digestion and absorption happen in the small intestine,
whose first segment, the **duodenum**, receives the pancreatic juice and the bile.

Click each organ in the illustration below to see what happens to a meal there.

<div data-island="gut" data-src="/diagrams/gut-journey.yml"></div>

## Digestion: motility, enzymes and hormones {#sec-breakdown}

### Motility: moving the food {#sec-motility}

Muscle in the gut wall moves food in two patterns, and sphincters keep it moving forward:

Peristalsis
: Travelling waves of muscle contraction that push the **bolus** (the soft mass of chewed food and
  saliva) forward.

Segmentation
: Back-and-forth squeezing that mixes the contents with digestive juices, mainly in the small
  intestine.

Sphincters
: Rings of muscle (the lower oesophageal, pyloric, ileocaecal and anal sphincters) that stop contents
  moving backwards.

**Gastric emptying**, the passage of food from the stomach into the duodenum, is actively regulated. A
meal leaves the stomach over a few hours. Counter-intuitively, a fatty or large meal empties more
slowly, because signals from the duodenum slow gastric emptying; this is partly why a greasy meal "sits
heavy".
Between meals, a cyclical "housekeeper" wave, the **migrating motor complex**, sweeps leftovers and
bacteria onward roughly every 1–2 hours; the hormone motilin triggers it [@deloose2012mmc].

::: {.callout-note}
## How long does a meal take?
Transit times are coarse ranges, not fixed numbers: hours in the stomach, hours in the small
intestine, and up to a day or more in the colon, around 1–3 days end to end, varying with diet, fibre,
fluid and activity. (Fibre's effect on bowel regularity is in the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd)
chapter.)
:::

### Chemical digestion: enzymes along the gut {#sec-enzymes}

Each digestive enzyme is specific to one kind of nutrient, like a pair of scissors that cuts only one
material, and each works at a particular place along the gut [@statpearlsDigestion]. Digestion begins
in the mouth and ends at the **brush border**, the surface of the cells lining the small intestine,
where the last enzymes sit (see [the absorptive surface](#sec-surface)).

Four sites do the chemical work, each with its own enzymes and targets:

| Site | Made by | Enzyme or secretion | Breaks down |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mouth | salivary glands | salivary amylase; a little lingual lipase | starch → smaller sugars; a token start on fat |
| Stomach | chief cells / parietal cells | pepsin; hydrochloric acid + intrinsic factor | protein → peptides |
| Duodenum | pancreas | amylase, lipase (+ colipase), proteases; bicarbonate | starch, fat, protein → smaller units |
| Brush border | cells lining the small intestine | disaccharidases (lactase, sucrase, maltase); peptidases | sugars and peptides → absorbable units |

In the stomach, **parietal cells** make hydrochloric acid, which denatures protein and kills microbes.
They also make **intrinsic factor**, which is needed much further along the small intestine to absorb
vitamin B12. **Chief cells** make **pepsin**, the enzyme that cuts protein into peptides
[@statpearlsStomach].

Salivary **amylase**, which starts the digestion of starch, stops working once it meets the stomach's
acid. In the duodenum, the pancreas adds bicarbonate, which neutralises that acid. Neutralisation gives
the pancreatic enzymes the near-neutral pH they need.

The pancreatic enzymes then take over: amylase continues on starch, proteases cut protein, and
**lipase**, working with colipase, digests fat. At the brush border, **disaccharidases** (lactase,
sucrase, maltase) split disaccharides into single sugars, and **peptidases** finish the digestion of
protein.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why pancreatic proteases are secreted inactive
The pancreas makes its protein-digesting enzymes as inactive precursors (zymogens), which are activated
only once they reach the gut. Otherwise the enzymes would digest the pancreas itself. The concept matters here,
not the named activation cascade.
:::

### Lactase deficiency and lactose intolerance {#sec-lactose}

The brush-border enzyme lactase splits lactose (milk sugar; see the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd)
chapter). Most of the world's adults make less lactase after childhood, and this is the norm, not a
disease. Three conditions are easy to confuse:

Lactase deficiency
: Making little lactase; very common in East Asian adults.

Lactose intolerance
: Symptoms (bloating, wind) from a given amount of lactose. Most people tolerate the lactose in about
  a cup of milk [@nihConsensus2010].

Milk allergy
: An immune reaction to milk protein, unrelated to lactase.

The gap between the first two is wide. In Singapore-born Chinese adults, about 95% are
lactase-deficient, yet only around a third report symptoms on ordinary amounts of milk [@yap1989]. A
more recent multi-ethnic Malaysian study finds the same high prevalence across Chinese, Malay and
Indian adults [@goh2018lactase].

When undigested lactose reaches the colon, resident bacteria ferment it and produce gas (see the
[*Gut Microbiome*](gut-microbiome.qmd#sec-scfa) chapter). The practical message is food-first and
culturally aware: hard cheese, yoghurt, lactose-free milk and non-dairy calcium sources (calcium-set
tofu, fortified soy milk, leafy greens, small fish with bones) all work, while "just drink three
glasses of milk" does not.

### Gut hormones: timing secretion and motility {#sec-gut-hormones}

The gut is often called the body's largest endocrine organ: hormone-making cells are scattered singly
through its lining. The gut hormones share one logic: food arriving in one segment releases a hormone
that prepares the next stage or inhibits the one before [@statpearlsGIhormones]. Five gut hormones each
have one main job in secretion or motility (their role in appetite is in the [*Appetite & Weight
Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-gut-peptides) chapter):

| Hormone | Made by | Trigger | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gastrin | stomach (G cells) | protein in the stomach | ↑ stomach acid |
| Secretin | duodenum (S cells) | acid arriving in the duodenum | ↑ pancreatic bicarbonate; ↓ acid |
| Cholecystokinin (CCK) | duodenum (I cells) | fat and protein in the duodenum | ↑ pancreatic enzymes; contracts the gallbladder; slows gastric emptying |
| Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) | duodenum (K cells) | glucose and fat | amplifies insulin secretion after a meal (an incretin) |
| Motilin | small intestine (M cells) | fasting between meals | drives the migrating motor complex |

Glucose eaten raises insulin more than the same glucose given intravenously, because hormones released
by the gut in response to food amplify insulin secretion. This amplification is the **incretin effect**, carried by GIP and a
partner hormone, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) [@nauck2016incretin]. The same signal is the basis of
major modern diabetes and weight medicines (see the [*Appetite & Weight
Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd#sec-obesity) and [*Type 2 Diabetes*](type-2-diabetes.qmd)
chapters).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a fatty meal "sits heavy". Why does it leave the stomach more slowly than a small, low-fat meal?
Gastric emptying is regulated by signals from the duodenum. Fat and protein arriving there release
CCK, which stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion and also slows gastric
emptying. This is the general logic of the gut hormones: food arriving in one segment inhibits the
segment before it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: most Singapore-born Chinese adults are lactase-deficient, yet only about a third report symptoms on ordinary amounts of milk. How can both be true?
Lactase deficiency means making little lactase; lactose intolerance means having symptoms from a given
amount of lactose. Most lactase-deficient adults still tolerate the lactose in about a cup of milk, and
only about a third report symptoms on ordinary amounts. The practical advice therefore turns on amount
and food choice (hard cheese, yoghurt, lactose-free milk, non-dairy calcium sources).
:::

## Absorption across the gut wall {#sec-absorption}

### The absorptive surface {#sec-surface}

The small intestine's absorptive surface is far larger than its outside suggests. Its lining is thrown
into circular folds, the folds are carpeted with finger-like **villi**, and each lining cell carries a
fuzz of **microvilli**, which form the brush border. Together they give a surface of roughly 30 m²,
about half a badminton court.

![Circular folds, villi and microvilli amplify the absorptive surface. Micrograph: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0.](/figures/anatomy/small-intestine-histology.jpg){#fig-villi fig-alt="Histology of the small intestine showing circular folds, villi and the brush border of microvilli." width="420" .lightbox}

::: {.callout-warning}
## Is the gut's surface the size of a tennis court?
Textbooks long claimed that the gut's surface rivals a tennis court (~200–300 m²). Careful measurement
puts it at about 30–40 m²: large, but far smaller [@helander2014].
:::

### Four routes into the enterocyte {#sec-transport}

Each absorptive cell, or **enterocyte**, has two faces: the brush border faces the gut contents, and the
far side faces blood and lymph. Nutrients enter the enterocyte by one of four routes:

- passive diffusion, for fats and water;
- facilitated diffusion, for fructose, through glucose transporter 5 (GLUT5);
- primary active transport, by a pump that uses energy directly;
- **secondary active transport**, which uses an ion gradient that a pump has generated.

Glucose enters by secondary active transport, the route that oral rehydration depends on (see [Oral
rehydration](#sec-ors)). A sodium pump keeps sodium low inside the enterocyte, and the resulting sodium
gradient acts like a battery: **sodium–glucose cotransporter 1 (SGLT1)** uses it to carry glucose into
the cell alongside sodium [@roder2014]. Absorbed sugars and amino acids (and small peptides) drain
into the **portal vein**, which carries them to the liver first.

### Fat absorption: bile, micelles and the lymphatic route {#sec-fat-absorption}

Fat needs special handling because it does not dissolve in water. Four terms describe how it is
absorbed:

Bile salts
: Detergents made by the liver from cholesterol that emulsify fat, breaking it into tiny droplets that
  lipase can reach.

Mixed micelles
: Clusters of bile salts and the products of fat digestion that carry those products to the brush
  border.

Chylomicron
: A particle of reassembled fat packaged with cholesterol and protein inside the enterocyte, too big to
  enter a blood capillary.

Lacteal
: A lymph vessel that takes up chylomicrons from the gut.

Bile salts emulsify the fat, lipase digests it, and the products cluster with bile salts into mixed
micelles that carry them to the brush border. There the fat diffuses into the enterocyte and the
micelle stays behind: it acts as a shuttle and is not itself absorbed. Inside the cell the fat is
re-esterified (reassembled into triglyceride; see the [*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd)
chapter) and packaged into chylomicrons. Because a chylomicron is too big for a blood capillary, it enters a lacteal and reaches
the blood through the lymph, bypassing the liver's first pass. This is why blood drawn after a fatty
meal can look faintly milky.

![How dietary fat is absorbed: bile emulsifies it, micelles carry it to the gut wall, and it leaves as chylomicrons in the lymph. Diagram: Health in Medicine, CC BY-SA 4.0.](/figures/anatomy/fat-absorption.svg){#fig-fat fig-alt="Schematic of fat absorption: a fat droplet is emulsified by bile salts, digested by lipase, carried in micelles into the enterocyte, re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons that enter the lacteal; short- and medium-chain fatty acids enter blood directly." width="640" .lightbox}

Most dietary fat is long-chain and takes this lymphatic route. Short- and medium-chain fatty acids are
small enough to enter the blood directly, like sugars.

Bile salts can emulsify fat because of their shape. A bile salt has a water-loving face and a
fat-loving face (it is amphipathic, like the membrane phospholipids in the *Macronutrients* chapter),
so it can sit at the oil–water boundary and break fat apart. The model of cholic acid below shows
the two faces.

<div data-island="molecule" data-src="/structures/bile.mol.yml"></div>

### The enterohepatic circulation and the terminal ileum {#sec-bile}

Bile salts are recycled. The liver makes bile, the gallbladder stores and concentrates it, and CCK
releases it into the duodenum when a fatty meal arrives. About 95% of the bile salts are then
reabsorbed at the **terminal ileum**, the last stretch of the small intestine, and return to the liver
to be used again: the **enterohepatic circulation** [@chiang2013].

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-enterohepatic
%%| fig-cap: "The enterohepatic circulation: bile salts are recycled, not spent."
flowchart LR
  L["Liver<br/>makes bile from cholesterol"] --> G["Gallbladder<br/>stores &amp; concentrates"]
  G -->|"CCK, after a fatty meal"| D["Duodenum<br/>bile emulsifies fat"]
  D --> I["Terminal ileum<br/>~95% of bile salts reabsorbed"]
  I -->|"portal vein"| L
  I -. "~5% lost in stool<br/>(replaced by new synthesis)" .-> S["Excreted"]
```

The terminal ileum does two jobs: it reclaims bile salts, and it absorbs vitamin B12. Loss of or damage
to the terminal ileum can therefore cause both fat malabsorption and B12 deficiency.

::: {.callout-note}
## Sites of nutrient absorption
Absorption is often site-specific: iron in the duodenum, vitamin B12 (with intrinsic factor) at the
terminal ileum, and the fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) alongside fat and bile. A fat or bile problem
can therefore quietly cause deficiency of the fat-soluble vitamins too. (The nutrients themselves are
in the [*Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter.)
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why can blood drawn after a fatty meal look milky, when the glucose from the same meal goes to the liver first?
Sugars and amino acids drain into the portal vein, which takes them to the liver first. Long-chain fat
is re-esterified in the enterocyte and packaged into chylomicrons, which are too big for blood
capillaries, so they enter the lacteals and reach the blood through the lymph, bypassing the liver's
first pass. The chylomicrons in the blood give it the milky look.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: disease has damaged a patient's terminal ileum. Why might she develop both fat malabsorption and vitamin B12 deficiency?
The terminal ileum does two jobs. It reclaims about 95% of bile salts for reuse (the enterohepatic
circulation), so damage there lets bile salts escape and leaves less bile to emulsify fat. It is also
where vitamin B12, with intrinsic factor, is absorbed. One damaged site can therefore cause both problems.
:::

## Digestion and absorption in practice {#sec-in-practice}

### Food form, preparation and meal order {#sec-food-form}

The same food, with the same energy content, can be digested at different speeds. Its physical form,
how it is cooked, the order in which a meal's parts are eaten and what they are eaten with all change
how quickly it is digested and absorbed. The speed in turn sets how fast blood glucose rises and how
much satiety the meal generates, and for some nutrients these factors also change how much is absorbed
at all. (The blood-glucose response itself, the glycaemic index, is in the
[*Macronutrients*](macronutrients.qmd) chapter.)

Four changes to a meal alter its speed of digestion, mostly by changing gastric emptying or how easily
enzymes reach the food:

| What changes | Mechanism (why the speed changes) | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Whole → blended → juiced | Cell walls and starch granules hide substrate from enzymes; disrupting them exposes surface area, and liquids empty faster | Faster, higher glucose rise; less satiety |
| Cooking, then cooling | Heat gelatinises starch (faster); cooling forms resistant starch (slower), retained on reheating | Cooked faster; cooled rice/pasta a little slower |
| Vegetables and protein before carbohydrate | The pre-load slows gastric emptying and stimulates CCK and incretin release | A lower, flatter glucose peak |
| Adding fat, protein, fibre or acid to a carbohydrate | All slow gastric emptying; acid also slows brush-border sugar-splitting | Blunts the glucose rise |

**Form and the food matrix.** In an intact plant food, starch and sugars are enclosed within cell walls
and packed into semi-crystalline granules that enzymes cannot reach until the structure is broken (the
food matrix; see the *Macronutrients* chapter). Juicing, blending and fine milling rupture this matrix
and expose far more surface to amylase, and liquids leave the stomach faster than solids. Digestion is
therefore quicker, and the glucose peak higher and earlier, with less satiety, even when the sugar
content is unchanged. In a classic study, apples taken as juice produced a larger insulin response and
a rebound fall in glucose, and were the least satiating, compared with the whole fruit
[@haber1977apple]. A whole orange versus a glass of its juice makes the same point.

**Cooking, and cooling.** Heat and water gelatinise starch, swelling the granules and disrupting their
crystalline structure so that enzymes digest them more readily. Cooking also denatures protein and
improves its digestibility, by the same principle by which gastric acid unfolds protein for pepsin.
Cooling cooked starch partly reverses this: some retrogrades into resistant starch, which the small
intestine cannot digest and which passes to the colon (see the [*Gut Microbiome*](gut-microbiome.qmd#sec-scfa)
chapter). Chilling and reheating cooked rice or pasta therefore lowers their glycaemic response
modestly, and the resistant starch survives reheating [@sonia2015rice]. The effect is small and
variable, and is not a licence for larger portions.

**Meal order and accompanying foods.** With meal composition fixed, eating vegetables and protein before the
carbohydrate measurably lowers the post-meal glucose and insulin rise. In people with prediabetes
(blood glucose that has started to rise but is not yet in the diabetes range), a
vegetable-and-protein-first order reduced the glucose peak by roughly 45% relative to carbohydrate
first. The same order also reduced the incremental area under the curve, the post-meal rise above the
fasting level summed over time, by nearly 40%. These figures come from a single small, short-term study (15 adults with prediabetes, one meal in each
order), in line with earlier findings in type 2 diabetes, and data on long-term control are weaker [@shukla2019order]. The
vegetables and protein act as a pre-load: they slow gastric emptying of the carbohydrate and stimulate
the CCK and incretin responses described [above](#sec-gut-hormones).

Adding fat, protein, viscous fibre or acid to a carbohydrate meal has a similar effect through the same
slowing of gastric emptying. Vinegar is the best-studied acid: in a meta-analysis it modestly lowered
post-meal glucose and insulin [@shishehbor2017vinegar], probably by slowing gastric emptying and
inhibiting brush-border disaccharidases. These are adjuncts, not treatments.

**Processing.** Industrial processing performs much of the gut's mechanical work
(grinding, refining and gelatinising) before food is eaten. Ultra-processed foods (industrial
formulations made largely from refined ingredients and additives) are therefore digested faster and
more completely. Their soft textures are also eaten more quickly and signal satiety less
effectively, whereas eating more slowly and chewing more increase satiety modestly [@miquel2015chew].

::: {.callout-warning}
## What a controlled trial showed, and its limits
In a tightly controlled inpatient trial, 20 adults ate about 500 kcal/day more and gained weight on an
ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one. The diets were matched for calories presented,
macronutrients, sugar, fat, fibre and sodium, and eating rate was faster on the ultra-processed diet
[@hall2019upf]. The trial is important but small (n = 20) and brief (two weeks per arm) in a
metabolic-ward setting, and the mechanism is still debated (energy density, texture and eating rate are
all candidates). For digestion, the trial illustrates how processing changes the rate of eating and
digestion (its weight consequences are in the [*Appetite & Weight
Regulation*](appetite-weight-regulation.qmd) and [*Obesity & Metabolic
Syndrome*](obesity-metabolic-syndrome.qmd) chapters). Cooking, fermentation and freezing are also
processing, so not all processing is harmful; minimally processed foods keep the structure that slows
digestion.
:::

Viscous fibre acts twice, once on speed and once on bile. Viscous fibres such as oat β-glucan and
psyllium thicken the intestinal contents, slowing both gastric emptying and glucose absorption. They
also bind bile salts, so that more are lost in stool. To replace them, the liver draws cholesterol from the blood, which is why adequate
viscous fibre modestly lowers LDL cholesterol [@whitehead2014betaglucan]. This is the enterohepatic
circulation deliberately interrupted (fibre fermentation is a separate process; see the *Gut
Microbiome* chapter).

Fat also aids the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins. Vitamins A, D, E and K and the carotenoids (plant
pigments such as β-carotene) travel the same bile-and-micelle route as dietary fat, so a nearly
fat-free meal leaves much of them unabsorbed. Carotenoid uptake from a salad was negligible with a
fat-free dressing and rose with added fat [@brown2004carotenoid]. Only a little fat is needed, which is
a reason to dress vegetables with some oil rather than eat them fat-free (the vitamins themselves are
in the [*Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes*](04-micronutrients-hydration.qmd) chapter).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Food–drug interactions
Food can alter how a drug is absorbed by two broad mechanisms; at this stage the task is to recognise
and refer, not to manage.

The first is altered gut metabolism or transport. Grapefruit irreversibly inhibits intestinal
**CYP3A4**, the gut-wall enzyme that normally breaks down part of each dose of many drugs as they are absorbed, before they reach the bloodstream, and so raises
their blood levels. It is a rare case of a healthy food causing a clinically important interaction,
described for more than 85 medicines [@bailey2013grapefruit].

The second is binding, or **chelation**: calcium and iron, in dairy, supplements or antacids, can bind
certain drugs into a complex that cannot be absorbed. Calcium, for example, reduces levothyroxine
absorption [@singh2000levothyroxine], with similar effects for some antibiotics and bisphosphonates.
Separating them in time avoids the problem.

Alcohol is relevant here too. It injures the gastric lining and impairs absorption of several
nutrients, notably by blocking the active transport of thiamine, part of the mechanism behind thiamine
deficiency [@subramanya2010alcohol] (see the *Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes* chapter). The
priority is the habit rather than the list: with any new medicine, check the label and ask a
pharmacist about food, grapefruit, dairy, iron and timing.
:::

### Oral rehydration and SGLT1 {#sec-ors}

SGLT1 explains how a drink of glucose and sodium can treat dehydration. In severe diarrhoea (cholera,
rotavirus), the gut pours out fluid, but SGLT1 keeps working. SGLT1 cotransports sodium with glucose,
and water follows the sodium by osmosis, so a drink containing both glucose and sodium still gets fluid
in. As a result, a dehydrated child can be rehydrated by mouth, with no drip
needed.

::: {.flow}
[Why oral rehydration works]{.tree-title}

1. Glucose and sodium drink
2. SGLT1 carries both in
3. Water follows sodium
4. Rehydration by mouth
:::

That drink is **oral rehydration salts (ORS)**: the modern WHO formula is a precise, low-strength mix
of 75 mmol/L each of sodium and glucose [@whoORS2006]. The underlying discovery was called, in a 1978
*Lancet* editorial, "potentially the most important medical advance this century"
[@lancet1978water], and oral rehydration has since saved tens of millions of lives [@ourworldindataORT].

::: {.callout-warning}
## Does plain water rehydrate as well as ORS?
Water is the obvious drink for replacing lost fluid, but plain water lacks the glucose and sodium that
drive SGLT1. In ORS the glucose is there to be cotransported with sodium, not as a calorie source, and
that coupling is why ORS rehydrates better than plain water alone.
:::

### Common beliefs about digestion {#sec-digestion-beliefs}

Six common beliefs about digestion can be tested against the evidence:

- "Gluten-free is healthier for everyone." It is healthier only for people with **coeliac disease**
  (an immune reaction to gluten that damages the lining of the small intestine) or wheat allergy.
  Going gluten-free can cost fibre and micronutrients, and if coeliac disease is suspected, test for
  it before gluten is removed, or the test misleads [@glutenFreeNonCeliac].
- "I need to detox / my 'leaky gut' is the problem." The liver and kidneys already detoxify. The gut
  barrier is real, but "leaky gut syndrome" as a diagnosable, supplement-fixable disease is not
  established, and there is no reliable test for it [@leakyGutMechanisms].
- "Enzyme and probiotic supplements fix bloating for everyone." There is little evidence for them in
  healthy people. Enzymes help only in narrow cases (lactase, or Beano for beans), and probiotics are
  strain- and situation-specific, not a general tonic [@agaProbiotics2020].
- "Spicy food causes ulcers." Ulcers are caused by *Helicobacter pylori* and non-steroidal
  anti-inflammatory painkillers (NSAIDs), not chilli [@lanas2017pud].
- "Fruit juice or a smoothie is as good as whole fruit." Juicing removes the intact food matrix,
  speeding digestion and blunting satiety. Across large cohorts, whole fruit is associated with lower
  type 2 diabetes risk and fruit juice with higher [@muraki2013fruit].
- "Fat-free is the healthiest way to eat vegetables." For the fat-soluble vitamins and carotenoids, a
  nearly fat-free meal leaves much unabsorbed; a little fat improves their uptake
  [@brown2004carotenoid].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: two people eat the same mixed-rice plate, one rice first and the other vegetables and fish first. Why does the second get a lower, flatter glucose peak?
Eating the vegetables and protein first acts as a pre-load: it slows gastric emptying of the
carbohydrate that follows and stimulates the CCK and incretin responses, so the glucose arrives more
slowly. In a small, short-term study in people with prediabetes, this order lowered the glucose peak by
roughly 45%; data on long-term control are weaker.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does viscous fibre such as oat β-glucan modestly lower LDL cholesterol?
Viscous fibre binds bile salts in the gut, so more are lost in stool instead of being reclaimed at the
terminal ileum. To replace them, the liver draws cholesterol from the blood to make new bile salts,
which modestly lowers LDL cholesterol. The fibre works by interrupting the enterohepatic circulation.
:::

## What happens to a meal? {#sec-close}

A plate of mixed rice with vegetables and fish is first broken down and then absorbed, in five stages:

1. In the mouth, chewing forms a bolus and salivary amylase starts on the rice starch.
2. In the stomach, acid denatures the fish protein and pepsin cuts it into peptides, while the meal
   empties into the duodenum over a few hours.
3. In the duodenum, secretin and CCK stimulate the release of bicarbonate, pancreatic enzymes and
   bile, and the pancreatic enzymes break starch, fat and protein into smaller units.
4. At the brush border, the last enzymes finish the sugars and peptides. Glucose enters with sodium
   through SGLT1, and sugars and amino acids travel to the liver by the portal vein.
5. The fat, emulsified by bile and carried by micelles, leaves the enterocytes as chylomicrons in the
   lymph. Most of the bile salts are reclaimed at the terminal ileum, and the undigested remainder of
   the meal passes to the colon.

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

Three digestive mechanisms apply directly to practice in Singapore:

- Lactase deficiency is the local norm, not a disease. About 95% of Singapore-born Chinese adults are
  lactase-deficient, yet only about a third report symptoms from the milk in their usual diet [@yap1989], so the
  food-first options (hard cheese, yoghurt, lactose-free milk, calcium-set tofu, fortified soy milk;
  see [lactose intolerance](#sec-lactose)) matter far more here than advice to "just drink more milk".
- Meal order costs nothing to change at the hawker stall. At a mixed-rice (*cai png*) stall, eating
  the vegetables and the fish or tofu first and the rice last flattens the glucose rise
  [@shukla2019order].
- Oral rehydration salts, a pharmacy staple, use SGLT1 cotransport to rehydrate by mouth, without an
  intravenous drip, in the gastroenteritis every family meets.
